facts.text: The red-tailed hawk is a bird of prey and one of the most common hawks in North America.

facts.text: The green heron is a small heron of North and Central America.

In towns, among buildings and trees where it can nest and roost, huge, noisy flocks may gather near the roosts.
To win a mate, a little green trimming will do, so long as herbs are tucked among it.

tagline.text: Named after its own voice, a singer of tunes and machine sounds.

facts.text: The tree swallow is a migratory bird of the family Hirundinidae.
The tree swallow nests either in isolated pairs or loose groups, in both natural and artificial cavities.
Because of the large amount of research on the tree swallow and how it willingly breeds in nest boxes, biologist Jason Jones recommended that it be considered a model organism.
The tree swallow's song consists of three parts: the chirp, the whine, and the gurgle.
When a swallow returns to nest, it usually does not change breeding sites.
In some parts of the US, the range of this swallow has extended south, likely due to changes in land use, the reintroduction of beavers, and nest boxes installed for bluebirds.
According to a 1987 study, this likely allows a younger female to explore nest sites, as the resident male is usually less aggressive to a subadult female.
The female incubates the clutch of two to eight pure white eggs for around 14 to 15 days.
Its wingspan is about 32 cm.
It weighs about 21 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It nests in a cavity.
It lays 2 to 8 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Listen over the wetland: a chirp, a whine, a gurgle, the three parts of one song.
It nests in a hollow, natural or built by people, as a lone pair or in loose groups.
When it returns to nest, it seldom changes its breeding site.
In some parts of the US it has spread south, likely helped by returning beavers and boxes put up for bluebirds.
In the hollow, the female sits warming her clutch of pure white eggs.

tagline.text: Chirp, whine and gurgle, then home to the same hollow.

facts.text: The royal tern is a tern in the family Laridae.
The royal tern typically feeds in small secluded bodies of water such as estuaries, mangroves, and lagoons.
The royal tern nests on island beaches or isolated beaches with limited predators.
The western population nests from California to Mexico and winters from California south to Peru.
The royal tern has few predators when it is mature, but before the chicks hatch or while they are chicks the tern is threatened by humans, other animals, and the tides.
The entire crown is black with a shaggy, erectable crest on the nape in the spring during courtship and the start of the breeding season.
The royal tern feeds in salt water and on very rare occasions in fresh water.
It lays one or two eggs, usually in a scrape, an area on the ground where a tern has made a small hole to lay its eggs.
Its wingspan is about 115 cm.
It weighs about 415 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in the open sea.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It nests in a scrape on the ground.
It lays 1 to 2 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: On a lonely island beach, where few hunters come, the royal tern makes its nest: a small hole scraped in the ground.
There it lays one or two eggs, and there danger waits, for eggs and chicks are threatened by people, other animals and the tides.
Grown, the tern has few enemies.
In spring courtship, a shaggy black crest rises on its nape, a crown fit for its name.
It hunts in quiet salt waters: estuaries, mangroves and lagoons.

tagline.text: A black crown, a lonely beach, and quiet salt lagoons.

facts.text: The Sandwich tern is a tern in the family Laridae.
Young birds bear grey and blackish scalloped plumage on their backs and wings.
It nests in a ground scrape and lays one or two eggs.
The Sandwich tern is very vocal; its call is a characteristic loud grating kear-ik or kerr ink.
Like all Thalasseus terns, the Sandwich tern feeds by plunge-diving for fish, almost invariably from the sea.
It breeds in the Palearctic from Europe to the Caspian Sea, and winters in the Mediterranean and on the coasts of Africa, India, and Sri Lanka.
The terns are small to medium-sized seabirds, gull-like in appearance, but usually with a more delicate, lighter build and shorter, weaker legs.
Sandwich tern is a long-distance migrant.
Its wingspan is about 96 cm.
It weighs about 200 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in the open sea.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It nests in a scrape on the ground.
It lays 1 to 2 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Kear-ik, kerr ink: so rings the loud, grating call of a very vocal bird.
Light of build and short of leg, this seabird spends most of its time in the air.
It hunts by plunge-diving for fish, almost always from the sea.
Its nest is only a scrape in the ground, holding one or two eggs.
A far traveler, it breeds from Europe to the Caspian Sea and winters on the coasts of Africa and India.

tagline.text: A grating cry above the sea, then a plunge for fish.

facts.text: The Carolina wren is a species of wren common in the eastern United States, the extreme south of Ontario, Canada, the northeast and southeast of Mexico, and into northern Central America.
After finding a mate, pairs maintain a territory and stay together for several years.
One aspect of territorial defense involves identifying the proximity of the threat based on the loudness of bird song as well as the level of degradation of the calls.
Mate changing is rare, and there has been one possible observation of polygamy.
Carolina wrens sing year round and at any point during the daytime, except during the most harsh weather conditions.
Explanations given include infrequent winter storms in the 20th century, expanded forest habitats, and the wrens taking advantage of urban areas containing feeders, especially in winter.

Although Carolina wrens are fairly common, brood parasitism by the brown-headed cowbird is common, with up to 25% of Carolina wren nests being affected in certain regions such as Oklahoma and Alabama.
Song degradation can also be used to determine the proximity of potential intruders.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 18 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 19 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in woodland.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It lays 3 to 6 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Morning, noon or late afternoon, winter or summer, its song rings out, and only the harshest weather can hush it.
Once two birds pair, they keep a home ground together for several years, and they rarely trade partners.
Guarding that ground, they listen closely to a stranger's song.
A loud, clear song tells them the rival is near; a faint, worn one says it is still far off.

tagline.text: It sings through every season and hears how far trouble lies.

facts.text: The brown thrasher, sometimes erroneously called the brown thrush or fox-coloured thrush, is a bird in the family Mimidae, which also includes the New World catbirds and mockingbirds.
The brown thrasher is noted for having over 1,000 song types, and the largest song repertoire of birds.
When it feels bothered, it usually hides into thickets and gives cackling calls.
Brown thrashers are typically monogamous birds, but mate-switching does occur, at times during the same season.
The brown thrasher often vies for habitat and potential nesting grounds with other birds, which is usually initiated by the males.
Whenever these situations occur, the brown thrashers usually discard the cowbirds' eggs.
The brown thrasher is an omnivore, with its diet ranging from insects to fruits and nuts.
The brown thrasher has been noted for having an aggressive behavior, and is a staunch defender of its nest.
Its wingspan is about 33 cm.
It weighs about 69 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 6 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Over a thousand song types live in a single throat, the largest song collection known among birds.
Yet when trouble comes, the great singer slips away into the thickets and gives only cackling calls.
It quarrels with other birds for places to live and nest, and it is the males who usually start the fight.
Its cup of a nest it guards fiercely, a staunch defender to the end.
Even cowbirds' eggs, it usually throws away.

tagline.text: A giant songbook, and a fierce guard at the nest.

facts.text: The greater yellowlegs is a large shorebird in the family Scolopacidae.
They mainly eat insects and small fish, as well as crustaceans, marine worms, frogs, seeds and berries.
They nest on the ground, usually in well-hidden locations near water.
The call is harsher, louder, and clearer than that of the lesser yellowlegs.
The young leave the nest within 24 hours of hatching and then leave the vicinity of the nest within two days.
Their breeding habitat is bogs and marshes in the boreal forest region of Canada and Alaska.
They migrate to the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the United States, the Caribbean, and south to South America.
The greater yellowlegs is similar in appearance to the smaller lesser yellowlegs.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 64 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 162 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Near Threatened.

sentences.text: Across the bogs and marshes of the northern forest rings a call harsher, louder and clearer than its smaller cousin's.
It belongs to the greater yellowlegs, a large shorebird that nests on the ground, well hidden near water.
Its chicks waste no time: they leave the nest within a day of hatching and soon wander far from it.
Then the bird flies on to the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, the Caribbean, and south to South America.

tagline.text: The loud-voiced shorebird of the northern bogs.

facts.text: The willet is a large shorebird in the family Scolopacidae.
They are territorial both on the breeding grounds and on the wintering areas but form loose breeding colonies or wintering groups.
The male normally leads the female through the territory and creates trial nest scrapes for the female to consider until she selects the site.
The willet's name is onomatopoeic and refers to its loud piercing "pill-will-willet" territorial song., which is higher pitched and repeated at a faster rate in Eastern willets than in Western birds.
The passage of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act in 1918 protected the willet from intensive exploitation by hunters for food and allowed its numbers to rebound to present levels.
When displaying the wings are held stiffly and downcurved in flight while on the ground the display gives prominence to the distinctive pattern of the underwings.
If the nest is placed among grass the female may pull grass stalks over the nest for camouflage.
The eastern willet breeds in coastal saltmarshes while the western willet breeds in freshwater prairie marshes, sloughs, potholes and other inland wetlands.
Its wingspan is about 70 cm.
It weighs about 246 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in coasts.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Pill-will-willet rings across the marsh, and so the bird named itself, for "willet" echoes that loud, piercing song.
Eastern birds, bred in coastal saltmarshes, sing it higher and faster than western birds of inland prairie marshes.
The male leads the female through his territory, scratching trial nest scrapes until she picks one.
Among grass, she may pull stalks over the nest to hide it.
A loud voice for the ground it claims, and a hidden home.

tagline.text: It sings its own name across the marsh.

facts.text: The American robin is a migratory bird of the true thrush genus and Turdidae, the wider thrush family.
The species is active mostly during the day and assembles in large flocks at night.
The species is one of the first North American birds to lay eggs, and normally has two to three broods per breeding season, which lasts from April to July.
The male, as with many thrushes, has a complex and almost continuous song.
The Tlingit people of northwestern North America held it to be a culture hero created by Raven to please the people with its song.
Juveniles and eggs are preyed upon by squirrels, snakes, and some birds.
Its diet consists of invertebrates, fruits, and berries.
The flocks break up during the day when the birds feed on fruits and berries in smaller groups.
Its wingspan is about 39 cm.
It weighs about 78 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: By night the robins gather in great flocks; by day the flocks break apart, and small bands go seeking fruit and berries.
Few North American birds lay eggs sooner, and the robin raises brood after brood from April to July.
And the male sings, his song complex and almost without pause.
The Tlingit people of northwestern North America held that Raven made the robin to please the people with that song.

tagline.text: The thrush that Raven made to sing.

facts.text: The eastern kingbird is a large tyrant flycatcher native to the Americas.
Eastern kingbirds are conspicuous and are commonly found in open areas with scattered trees and bushes, where they perch while foraging for insects.
Eastern kingbirds wait on an open perch and fly out to catch insects in flight, sometimes hovering to pick prey off vegetation.
Eastern kingbirds in southern British Columbia may nest in open fields, in shrubs over open water, high up in trees, and even in the tops of small stumps.
They make a sturdy cup nest in a tree or shrub, sometimes on top of a stump or pole.
The call is a high-pitched, buzzing and unmusical chirp, frequently compared to an electric fence.
The aggressive mobbing behavior of eastern kingbirds has been shown to keep ravens and crows from finding experimental nests placed near kingbird nests.
Their breeding habitat is open areas across North America.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 35 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 40 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in woodland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: A buzz like an electric fence crackles across open country, a high, unmusical chirp from a bird perched in plain sight.
It waits there, darts out to snatch insects in flight, or hovers to pluck them off leaves.
Its nest is a sturdy cup in a tree or shrub, sometimes set atop a stump or pole.
When ravens and crows come near, it mobs them so fiercely that even nests beside its own stay hidden from them.

tagline.text: It buzzes like a fence and drives off ravens and crows.

facts.text: The white-eyed vireo is a small songbird of the family Vireonidae.

During the breeding season, the diet of this species consists almost exclusively of insects, primarily caterpillars and stink bugs; beetles, flies, wasps, snails, and very rarely small vertebrates are also consumed.
They nest near the ground in tangled thickets.
The white-eyed vireo's song is highly variable, consisting of a rapid series of notes bookended by sharp 'chip' notes.
V. g. bermudianus is endemic to Bermuda, where it is known as the Chick of the Village.
In the autumn and winter it supplements its diet of insects with berries.
Nests are made of weeds, leaves, grass, bark or bits of trash.
Populations on the US Gulf Coast and further south are resident, but most North American birds migrate south in winter.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 19 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 11 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a hanging nest.
It lays 3 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: On Bermuda, one small songbird goes by a homely name: the Chick of the Village.
Its song shifts and changes: a rapid run of notes bookended by sharp chips.
Close to the ground, in tangled thickets, it builds a nest of weeds, leaves, grass, bark or bits of trash.
Through the breeding season it hunts insects, mostly caterpillars and stink bugs.
In autumn and winter it adds berries; most North American birds fly south, though Gulf Coast birds stay.

tagline.text: A nest of trash and grass, low in the tangle.

facts.text: The red-eyed vireo is a small American songbird.
In their summer range they are primarily insectavores, using a high protein diet to fuel their young and build fat reserves for their eventual migration south.
They usually sing high up in trees for long periods of time in a question-and-answer rhythm.
Red-eyed vireos glean insects from tree foliage, primarily favoring caterpillars, beetles, and aphids, that they sometimes snatch while hovering.
Songs generally consist of 1–5 syllables between 2 and 6 kHz.
Adults are mainly olive-green on the upper parts with white underparts; they have a red iris and a grey crown edged with black.
It is somewhat warbler-like but not closely related to the New World warblers.
They have thick blue-grey legs and a stout bill.
Its wingspan is about 24 cm.
It weighs about 16 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 1 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: High in the trees, a small American songbird sings for long stretches in a question-and-answer rhythm.
It works the leaves as well, gleaning caterpillars, beetles and aphids, sometimes snatching one while it hovers.
In summer it lives mostly on insects, a high-protein diet that fuels its young.
It builds fat reserves too, saving them for its journey south.
Olive-green above and white below, it keeps to the forest with a red eye.

tagline.text: High in the trees, a song of question and answer.

facts.text: The blue-headed vireo is a migratory songbird found in North and Central America.
Blue-headed vireos are mainly insectivorous birds but are also known to eat fleshy berries and fruit.
When arriving to the breeding ground in mid-April, male vireos will hold large, individual territories that can range from 1.5–6.6 hectares.
The primary song of the blue-headed vireo is a simple, slow, monotonous tune that is often confused with the faster red-eyed vireo song.
During migration, blue-headed vireos are often found to flock with groups of different sparrow species but rarely with members of its own species.
They are equipped with short, strong bills used for processing insect prey with a tough carapace such as beetles.
Females will choose a male to mate with depending on the male's ability to defend and control a large territory.
The primary song is sung only by the males and usually only during the breeding season.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 23 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 15 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 3 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Mid-April brings the males back to the breeding grounds, and each claims a large territory of his own.
There he sings a simple, slow tune, over and over, and only in the breeding season.
Listeners often mistake it for the faster song of the red-eyed vireo.
Females choose their mate by how well he can defend and control so wide a ground.
On migration it travels with flocks of sparrows, but rarely with its own kind.

tagline.text: A slow song sung over a wide domain.

facts.text: The white-winged dove is a dove whose native range extends from the Southwestern United States through Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean.
The call is likened to the English phrase "who cooks for you".
Normally, up to 4000 birds are seen migrating, but in Texas, a flock of up to a million birds was recorded.
Males may aggressively defend territory from other males, sparring with wing slaps.
White-winged doves are popular as game birds for hunting.
In recent years with increasing urbanization and backyard feeding, it has expanded throughout Texas, into Oklahoma, Louisiana, and coastal Mississippi.
White-winged doves are subjected to the usual arid-land predators, including foxes, bobcats, snakes, and coyotes.
Their diet consists mostly of grains, but will also include pollen and nectar, especially from the saguaro cactus, which is a vital source of water.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 49 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 153 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It stays in its range all year.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a platform.
It lays 2 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Out where the saguaro stands, this bird sips the cactus's pollen and nectar, a vital source of water.
Mostly, though, it eats grains.
Its call, folks say, sounds like a question: who cooks for you?
Males may fiercely guard their ground from other males, sparring with slaps of the wing.
And as towns grew and backyards set out food, it spread across Texas and on into Oklahoma, Louisiana and coastal Mississippi.

tagline.text: It sips from the cactus and calls, who cooks for you?

facts.text: The mourning dove is a member of the dove family, Columbidae.
Mourning doves eat almost exclusively seeds, but the young are fed crop milk by their parents.
Outside the breeding season, mourning doves roost communally in dense deciduous trees or conifers.
Courtship begins with a noisy flight by the male, followed by a graceful, circular glide with outstretched wings and head down.
During the call, the throat of the dove swells.
The "mourning" part of its common name comes from its doleful call.
Migration is usually during the day, in flocks, and at low altitudes.
As a gamebird, the mourning dove is well-managed, with more than 20 million shot by hunters each year.
Its wingspan is about 43 cm.
It weighs about 119 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in towns, farms and other places people have changed.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 2 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: The mourning dove wears its name for its call, a doleful song.
As it sings, its throat swells round with the sound.
To win a mate, the male bursts up in a noisy flight, then glides in a graceful circle, wings stretched wide and head bowed down.
Seeds are nearly all it eats, yet its young are fed crop milk by their parents.
When the breeding season ends, the doves gather to roost together in dense trees.

tagline.text: A sorrowful song, a swelling throat, a graceful circling glide.

facts.text: The white-throated sparrow is a passerine bird of the New World sparrow family Passerellidae.
They mainly eat seeds, insects and berries, and are attracted to bird feeders.
They nest either on the ground under shrubs or low in trees in deciduous or mixed forest areas and lay three to five brown-marked blue or green-white eggs.
White-throated sparrows produce song laterally through the left side of their syrinx, and control of their syrinx involves both their central and peripheral nervous systems.
Alongside some other species such as the cardinal, dark-eyed junco, song sparrow and chickadees, this species ranks among the most abundant native birds during winter in eastern North America.
Blackberries, grapes, and rose hips are some fruits they eat.
Tan males invest in parental care and guard their mates from others searching for extra pair copulations.
The second song consists of an initial note, a second a whole step lower, and a third note, repeated two or three times, about a minor third below that.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 22 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 24 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in woodland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 1 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: A note, then one a whole step lower, then a last note falling lower still and repeated: so runs one of its songs.
It sings through the left side of its syrinx, its voice box.
It nests on the ground under shrubs or low in trees, laying brown-marked blue or green-white eggs.
Seeds, insects and berries such as blackberries, grapes and rose hips feed it.
Come winter in eastern North America, it ranks among the most plentiful native birds.

tagline.text: A falling song, sung from one side of its voice.
